paper.title: The moving parts of life: a meso-level analysis of interregional migration patterns after life course events
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement is printed. The paper states: …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish population register data / Danish Civil Registration System (CPR)
registers.role: sample frame, household-individual linkage, residential moves between (sub-)municipalities, deaths (widowhood)
treatment/event definition: start of a labor-market qualifying education and graduation
event definition: labor market entry after graduation and retirement (receipt of public pensions or early retirement benefits while not listed in AMR)

registers.name_in_paper: registers on education, tax, and labor market activities (register data from Statistics Denmark 2016)
registers.role: event definitions and regional context factors

registers.name_in_paper: regional data from Statistikbanken.dk and Noegletal.dk
registers.role: controls: municipal and sub-municipal context factors (unemployment, disposable income, industrial employment share, house prices, rental share, summer houses, thefts, kindergarten tuition, education and student shares, population, distance)

linkages: Individual persons and households are linked through a unique household ID (Danish Civil Registration System: a household is all individuals living at the same residential address who share common living arrangements)
Life events are identified at the household level and migration flow matrices are built from individual counts (persons)

Individual migration data are aggregated to origin-destination migration flow matrices between sub-municipalities (parishes) grouped into four settlement-size categories within each of the 98 Danish municipalities (LAU1)
Municipal-level context factors (labor market, housing, public services, amenities, distance) are joined to the sub-municipal flow pairs in a nested modelling framework (Fig. 1)

sample.universe: the full Danish population of approx. 5.1 million residents grouped into approx. 2.5 million households, 2007-2012 (Table 1 reports 5,108,777 persons and 1,784,395 migrants)
sample.unit_of_observation: origin-destination pair of sub-municipal settlement categories (destination i x origin j), one observation per pair per event group
selection_rules: Eight mutually exclusive life events are defined for 2007-2012 through logical conditions at the household level; no household in a given group experiences multiple events during the observation period
Households experiencing two or more overlapping events form the 'mixed events' reference group; households with none of the eight events form the 'no event' reference group
Sub-municipalities (parishes) are grouped within each municipality into four settlement categories: 100,000+ inhabitants; 10,000 to under 100,000; 1,000 to under 10,000; under 1,000

Of the (98 x 4) x ((98 - 1) x 4) = 152,096 possible origin-destination sub-municipal pairs, the 67,860 pairs with observed actual migration flows are used, because some municipalities lack certain settlement types
sample.n_observations: 67,860 origin-destination sub-municipal pairs per event-group regression
sample.n_individuals: 5,108,777 persons in the total population; 1,784,395 migrants (Table 1)

construction_notes: Life events are measured at the household level; when a student moves out of the parental home they are recorded as forming a new household at the new address and the event is measured for the newly formed household
Parents are counted as empty nesters when the last child leaves the parental household
Graduation requires finalizing a formal education according to UDDA and first registration in the Danish Labor Market Registers (AMR)
Partnership and divorce imply that two households merge into one (or split into two); for divorce both the old and the new household are included in the event group
Retirement is defined as receiving public pensions or early retirement benefits while not being listed in the AMR register
Widowhood: the surviving partner's household status is updated when a spouse dies (death date recorded in the CPR)
Both life events and migratory movements are measured at an annual scale; movements in the same and later years are assumed to be associated with the event
All regional context factors are relative regional differences, D.y_ij = y_i - y_j, in logs; distance and population levels also in logs
Migration, population size and population structure (education/student shares) are measured at the sub-municipal level; all other context factors at the municipal level

claims.statement: In a negative binomial model of event-group-specific interregional migration flows, D.unemp_ij is positively associated with MIG^Education_ij.

register_source.value: Statistics Denmark register data combined with regional data from Statistikbanken.dk and Noegletal.dk (no DST register code given in the paper)

definition.value: Difference in unemployment rate between i and j (in logs). Suffix 'D.' indicates relative regional differences, e.g. D.y_ij = y_i - y_j; measured at the municipal level at t(0), the start of the migration period.

timing.value: measured at t(0), i.e. at the beginning of the migration period t(1)-t(0) over 2007-2012

register_source.value: Danish population register data from Statistics Denmark (2016); migration counts of persons with life events identified at the household level via the household ID of the Danish Civil Registration System (CPR); no DST register code given

definition.value: Gross migration to i from j (event group: education): gross migration flow (count of persons) to sub-municipal region i from sub-municipal region j over the period t(1)-t(0) within 2007-2012, counted for households in which at least one household member starts a labor-market qualifying formal education and the individuals in the household migrate to region i from j.

timing.value: migration flows measured over t(1)-t(0), i.e. in the same year as the life event or later, within the 2007-2012 observation window

units.value: elasticity: change in log expected gross migration count (persons) per one-log-point increase in the regressor (log difference between i and j)

estimand.target_population: interregional (sub-municipal origin-destination) gross migration flows of Danish households in the Education event group, 2007-2012
estimand.time_horizon: gross migration flows cumulated over the period t(1)-t(0) within 2007-2012, with regional context factors measured at t(0)

population.description: Origin-destination pairs of sub-municipal settlement categories in the 98 Danish municipalities, with gross migration flows of persons in households for which at least one household member starts a labor-market qualifying formal education and the individuals in the household migrate to region i from j. Flows are built from the full Danish population of approx. 5.1 million persons in approx. 2.5 million households; Table 1 reports 210,348 registered persons and 141,625 migrants in this event group.
subgroups_defined: eight non-overlapping life course event groups (education, graduation, partnership, children, divorce, empty nest, retirement, widowhood)
two reference groups: mixed events and no event
four sub-municipal settlement size categories within each municipality
population.selection: only the 67,860 origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows, out of (98x4)x((98-1)x4)=152,096 possible pairs, because some municipalities lack certain settlement types

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional variation across 67,860 origin-destination sub-municipal pairs in regional context factors (differences between destination i and origin j), within an event-group-specific gravity-type count model; no reform or exogenous shock is used for identification

key_assumptions.assumption: The migration count is generated by a zero-inflated negative binomial process: exp(u^e_ij) ~ Gamma(1/tau, tau) in the count part and epsilon^e_ij ~ N(0, sigma^2) in the probit zero part, with the conditional mean exponential in the regressors (Eqs. (2) and (3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: pre-estimation tests of skewness, kurtosis and normality (Shapiro-Francia, Table A2); LR test of tau = 0 rejecting Poisson in favour of NegBin; significant Vuong (1989) z-statistic favouring the two-part (zero-inflated) model, both reported in Table 3

key_assumptions.assumption: Migratory movements observed in the same year as, or later than, a life event within the sample period are associated with (attributable to) that event.
key_assumptions.supported_by: none offered; the paper flags the annual measurement scale of events and moves as a limitation

key_assumptions.assumption: Each estimation column conditions the migration flow on a single, non-overlapping life event group: no household in a given group experiences more than one of the eight events during the observation period, which the authors argue minimizes bias from confounding events and from latent group heterogeneity (age, income, education, nationality, household type).
key_assumptions.supported_by: the event-group construction rules and the population size (Table 1); columns IX and X report mixed-event and no-event reference groups for comparison

implies_edges.from: life event group e (household experiences only event e)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the flow in MIG^e_ij

key_assumptions.assumption: Only origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows enter the estimation sample (67,860 of the 152,096 possible pairs), because some municipalities lack certain settlement types.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated construction of the flow matrices; the excess-zero component of Eq. (3) models remaining zero flows

implies_edges.from: existence of a settlement type pair (i,j)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the pair in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated coefficients are associations, not causal effects: the authors state that the identified correlations should not be interpreted as strict causal links at the regional aggregate level.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicit caveat in the results section and in the conclusion

threats_discussed: latent group heterogeneity (age, income, education, nationality, household type) when life events are pooled
annual measurement scale of both life events and migratory movements
settlement structure within municipalities as a latent influence on migration flows, addressed by the nested sub-municipal modelling framework
excess zero migration flows between sub-municipal pairs, addressed by the two-part (zero-inflated) NegBin model
spatial autocorrelation of net migration rates (Moran's I, Table A1), judged low to moderate
robustness_checks: pre-estimation tests of skewness, kurtosis and normality (Shapiro-Francia), Table A2
LR test of the dispersion parameter tau = 0 (Poisson vs NegBin), reported in Table 3
Vuong (1989) test of ZINB vs NegBin, reported in Table 3
binary probit regressions for zero migration flows (Table A21, online appendix)
pairwise Wald tests for coefficient equality across event groups (Table 4; Tables A3-A20)
Moran's I spatial autocorrelation tests (Table A1)
unresolved_confounders: the authors state that the identified correlations should not be interpreted as strict causal links at the regional aggregate level, and name no specific confounder they adjust for

estimator.value: zero-inflated negative binomial (two-part NegBin count model, Eqs. (2) and (3)), maximum likelihood

estimation.specification: Nested (sub-municipal within municipal) gravity-type count model of event-group-specific gross migration flows, Eq. (2) with zero-inflation component Eq. (3); all regional context factors enter as origin-destination differences in logs; a constant term is included but not reported
estimation.clustering: none stated; heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are reported in parentheses

heterogeneity.finding: Pairwise Wald tests for coefficient equality across event groups (Table 4, p. 22) reject equality for between 44% (empty nest vs retirement) and 94% (education vs partnership) of the variables in the migration model.

links.pointer_quote: Our findings corroborate theoretical model predictions and prior evidence that migration across life-event groups responds heterogeneously to regional labor market conditions, with interregional migrants in the transition from job-qualifying education to work responding most strongly to local economic signals.
As Panels A and B show, local labor market differences are particularly relevant for migration associated with graduation and entering the labor market

links.pointer_quote: Recreational amenities attract empty-nesters and retiring households, whereas newly formed couples and young families move to neighborhoods with affordable housing, high-quality pre-school education and low crime rates.

Over the life cycle, interregional migration after family transitions such as forming a legally recognized partnership, child-bearing, and the "empty nest" phase are comparably stronger influenced by regional housing market conditions, local population structures and public service provision or place-based amenities.

links.pointer_quote: Recreational amenities attract empty-nesters and retiring households, whereas newly formed couples and young families move to neighborhoods with affordable housing, high-quality pre-school education and low crime rates.

Over the life cycle, interregional migration after family transitions such as forming a legally recognized partnership, child-bearing, and the "empty nest" phase are comparably stronger influenced by regional housing market conditions, local population structures and public service provision or place-based amenities.

population.description: Origin-destination pairs of sub-municipal settlement categories in the 98 Danish municipalities, with gross migration flows of persons in households for which two adult individuals initially constituting different households join into one household through marriage or legally recognized cohabitation and the individuals in the new household migrate to region i from j. Flows are built from the full Danish population of approx. 5.1 million persons in approx. 2.5 million households; Table 1 reports 234,152 registered persons and 89,473 migrants in this event group.
subgroups_defined: eight non-overlapping life course event groups (education, graduation, partnership, children, divorce, empty nest, retirement, widowhood)
two reference groups: mixed events and no event
four sub-municipal settlement size categories within each municipality
population.selection: only the 67,860 origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows, out of (98x4)x((98-1)x4)=152,096 possible pairs, because some municipalities lack certain settlement types

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional variation in whether the destination and/or origin municipality belongs to the 50 municipalities selected in 2004 for the Danish commuter tax allowance (tax exemption) scheme; the policy is already in place throughout the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: The migration count is generated by a zero-inflated negative binomial process: exp(u^e_ij) ~ Gamma(1/tau, tau) in the count part and epsilon^e_ij ~ N(0, sigma^2) in the probit zero part, with the conditional mean exponential in the regressors (Eqs. (2) and (3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: pre-estimation tests of skewness, kurtosis and normality (Shapiro-Francia, Table A2); LR test of tau = 0 rejecting Poisson in favour of NegBin; significant Vuong (1989) z-statistic favouring the two-part (zero-inflated) model, both reported in Table 3

key_assumptions.assumption: Migratory movements observed in the same year as, or later than, a life event within the sample period are associated with (attributable to) that event.
key_assumptions.supported_by: none offered; the paper flags the annual measurement scale of events and moves as a limitation

key_assumptions.assumption: Each estimation column conditions the migration flow on a single, non-overlapping life event group: no household in a given group experiences more than one of the eight events during the observation period, which the authors argue minimizes bias from confounding events and from latent group heterogeneity (age, income, education, nationality, household type).
key_assumptions.supported_by: the event-group construction rules and the population size (Table 1); columns IX and X report mixed-event and no-event reference groups for comparison

implies_edges.from: life event group e (household experiences only event e)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the flow in MIG^e_ij

key_assumptions.assumption: Only origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows enter the estimation sample (67,860 of the 152,096 possible pairs), because some municipalities lack certain settlement types.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated construction of the flow matrices; the excess-zero component of Eq. (3) models remaining zero flows

implies_edges.from: existence of a settlement type pair (i,j)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the pair in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated coefficients are associations, not causal effects: the authors state that the identified correlations should not be interpreted as strict causal links at the regional aggregate level.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicit caveat in the results section and in the conclusion

key_assumptions.assumption: The commuter tax allowance dummies cannot be read as a with-without treatment comparison: the policy is already in place throughout the 2007-2012 estimation sample and pre-treatment differences between municipalities are not considered.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicitly stated; the authors note that pre-treatment data are unavailable because of the 2006 Danish territorial reform

annual measurement scale of both life events and migratory movements
settlement structure within municipalities as a latent influence on migration flows, addressed by the nested sub-municipal modelling framework

spatial autocorrelation of net migration rates (Moran's I, Table A1), judged low to moderate

definition.value: Difference between the estimated coefficients on commuter_tax_i and commuter_tax_j; the variation arrives from two alternatives: (1) the destination region i is treated but the origin region j is not, (2) the origin region j is treated but the destination region i is not (otherwise the difference of the two dummies is always zero)

timing.value: the reform was established in 2004 and is already in place throughout the 2007-2012 estimation sample

register_source.value: Danish population register data from Statistics Denmark (2016); migration counts of persons with life events identified at the household level via the household ID of the Danish Civil Registration System (CPR); no DST register code given

definition.value: Gross migration to i from j (event group: graduation): gross migration flow (count of persons) to sub-municipal region i from sub-municipal region j over the period t(1)-t(0) within 2007-2012, counted for households in which at least one household member graduates from formal education and the individuals in the household migrate to region i from j.

timing.value: migration flows measured over t(1)-t(0), i.e. in the same year as the life event or later, within the 2007-2012 observation window

units.value: difference between two semi-elasticities: exp(D.commuter_tax_ij) is the Incidence Rate Ratio by which migration flows change when the destination is treated instead of the origin

magnitude.interpretation: Incidence Rate Ratio (IRR) reported in Table 6 for this event group: 0.91

estimand.target_population: interregional (sub-municipal origin-destination) gross migration flows of Danish households in the Graduation event group, 2007-2012
estimand.time_horizon: gross migration flows cumulated over the period t(1)-t(0) within 2007-2012, with regional context factors measured at t(0)

population.description: Origin-destination pairs of sub-municipal settlement categories in the 98 Danish municipalities, with gross migration flows of persons in households for which at least one household member graduates from formal education and the individuals in the household migrate to region i from j. Flows are built from the full Danish population of approx. 5.1 million persons in approx. 2.5 million households; Table 1 reports 213,524 registered persons and 119,184 migrants in this event group.
subgroups_defined: eight non-overlapping life course event groups (education, graduation, partnership, children, divorce, empty nest, retirement, widowhood)
two reference groups: mixed events and no event
four sub-municipal settlement size categories within each municipality
population.selection: only the 67,860 origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows, out of (98x4)x((98-1)x4)=152,096 possible pairs, because some municipalities lack certain settlement types

identification.source_of_variation: cross-sectional variation in whether the destination and/or origin municipality belongs to the 50 municipalities selected in 2004 for the Danish commuter tax allowance (tax exemption) scheme; the policy is already in place throughout the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: The migration count is generated by a zero-inflated negative binomial process: exp(u^e_ij) ~ Gamma(1/tau, tau) in the count part and epsilon^e_ij ~ N(0, sigma^2) in the probit zero part, with the conditional mean exponential in the regressors (Eqs. (2) and (3)).
key_assumptions.supported_by: pre-estimation tests of skewness, kurtosis and normality (Shapiro-Francia, Table A2); LR test of tau = 0 rejecting Poisson in favour of NegBin; significant Vuong (1989) z-statistic favouring the two-part (zero-inflated) model, both reported in Table 3

key_assumptions.assumption: Migratory movements observed in the same year as, or later than, a life event within the sample period are associated with (attributable to) that event.
key_assumptions.supported_by: none offered; the paper flags the annual measurement scale of events and moves as a limitation

key_assumptions.assumption: Each estimation column conditions the migration flow on a single, non-overlapping life event group: no household in a given group experiences more than one of the eight events during the observation period, which the authors argue minimizes bias from confounding events and from latent group heterogeneity (age, income, education, nationality, household type).
key_assumptions.supported_by: the event-group construction rules and the population size (Table 1); columns IX and X report mixed-event and no-event reference groups for comparison

implies_edges.from: life event group e (household experiences only event e)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the flow in MIG^e_ij

key_assumptions.assumption: Only origin-destination sub-municipal pairs with observed actual migration flows enter the estimation sample (67,860 of the 152,096 possible pairs), because some municipalities lack certain settlement types.
key_assumptions.supported_by: stated construction of the flow matrices; the excess-zero component of Eq. (3) models remaining zero flows

implies_edges.from: existence of a settlement type pair (i,j)
implies_edges.to: inclusion of the pair in the estimation sample

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimated coefficients are associations, not causal effects: the authors state that the identified correlations should not be interpreted as strict causal links at the regional aggregate level.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicit caveat in the results section and in the conclusion

key_assumptions.assumption: The commuter tax allowance dummies cannot be read as a with-without treatment comparison: the policy is already in place throughout the 2007-2012 estimation sample and pre-treatment differences between municipalities are not considered.
key_assumptions.supported_by: explicitly stated; the authors note that pre-treatment data are unavailable because of the 2006 Danish territorial reform

threats_discussed: latent group heterogeneity (age, income, education, nationality, household type) when life events are pooled
annual measurement scale of both life events and migratory movements
settlement structure within municipalities as a latent influence on migration flows, addressed by the nested sub-municipal modelling framework
excess zero migration flows between sub-municipal pairs, addressed by the two-part (zero-inflated) NegBin model
spatial autocorrelation of net migration rates (Moran's I, Table A1), judged low to moderate
robustness_checks: pre-estimation tests of skewness, kurtosis and normality (Shapiro-Francia), Table A2
LR test of the dispersion parameter tau = 0 (Poisson vs NegBin), reported in Table 3
Vuong (1989) test of ZINB vs NegBin, reported in Table 3
binary probit regressions for zero migration flows (Table A21, online appendix)
pairwise Wald tests for coefficient equality across event groups (Table 4; Tables A3-A20)
Moran's I spatial autocorrelation tests (Table A1)
unresolved_confounders: treatment endogeneity: the commuter tax allowance municipalities were selected on low economic growth, long commuting distances and lower income levels
no pre-treatment difference between treated and untreated municipalities can be modelled, because the 2006 Danish territorial reform means pre-policy data are unavailable

estimator.value: zero-inflated negative binomial (two-part NegBin count model, Eqs. (2) and (3)), maximum likelihood

estimation.specification: Nested (sub-municipal within municipal) gravity-type count model of event-group-specific gross migration flows, Eq. (2) with zero-inflation component Eq. (3); all regional context factors enter as origin-destination differences in logs; a constant term is included but not reported; extended by binary dummies for destination and origin municipalities treated by the commuter tax allowance reform
estimation.clustering: none stated; heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors are reported in parentheses

heterogeneity.finding: Table 6 reports the coefficient difference for each of the eight event groups separately; only for the education group is the difference positive and significant (IRR 1.17), while for graduation, partnership and widowhood it is negative and for child, divorce, empty nest and retirement it is insignificant.

evidence.how: Eq. (2) models the conditional mean of the migration count as exp(linear index); the regressor is a binary dummy, so the coefficient is a semi-elasticity (log incidence rate ratio) of expected gross migration flow.
